items.title: Energy of Alpha and Beta Particles in Radioactive Decay

source_refs.note: Energy of Alpha and Beta Particles in Radioactive Decay: a main subheading of 12.4 Radioactivity, its own page (owner 2026-11-04); PDF 266-269.

blocks.text: In both α-decay and β-decay, for a particular radionuclide, the same amount of energy is released. In a α-decay of a particular radionuclide, every emitted α-particle has the same sharply defined kinetic energy. When the number of α-particles is plotted against kinetic energy, there are distinct spikes that appear on the graph as shown in Fig. 12.5. This demonstrates that α-particles have discrete energies.

blocks.alt: A graph of the number of alpha particles (N) against kinetic energy (eV). Instead of a curve it shows four separate vertical spikes of different heights at particular energies.
blocks.caption: Figure 12.5: Discrete energy values of alpha-particles (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 12.5).

blocks.text: However, in the case of β-particle emission, energy is shared between β-particle and anti-neutrino in varying proportions. The sum of electron (or positron) energy and the anti-neutrino's (or neutrino's) energy, however, in every case remains the same. Thus in β-decay, the energy of an electron or a positron may range from zero to a maximum value. When the number of β-particles is plotted against kinetic energy, the graph shows a curve as shown in Fig. 12.6. This demonstrates that beta particles (electrons or positrons) have a continuous range of energies. The principle of conservation of momentum and energy applies in both alpha and beta emission.

blocks.alt: A graph of the number of beta particles (N) against kinetic energy (eV). A smooth continuous curve starts part-way up the vertical axis, rises to a peak at a low energy, then falls and tails off to zero at the highest energy.
blocks.caption: Figure 12.6: Continuous spectrum of beta-particles (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 12.6).

blocks.text: The emission of γ-radiation from a nucleus is generally represented by this equation:

blocks.text_alt: ᴬ_Z X* → ᴬ_Z X + γ radiation

blocks.text: where ᴬ_Z X* represents an excited nucleus while ᴬ_Z X shows ground state of the nucleus.
